manifest.prompt: a 2D physics sandbox where you can drag boxes around
consumers: check an output against the dump
how_to_read: 1. Read the head first: the first 33 lines hold manifest, essence and routing (Read limit=33, or jq '{manifest, essence, routing}' physics-sandbox.metadump.json).
2. Pick the route for your job and run its jq: jq '<routing[i].jq>' physics-sandbox.metadump.json
3. Also pull the anti-keywords and review prompts (checks) for your scope: jq '.anti_keywords, .checks' physics-sandbox.metadump.json
4. Look up any term (lowercase): jq '.index["<term>"]' physics-sandbox.metadump.json  -> hits give id + path; not_meant lists senses to avoid.
5. Grep works too: every entry is one line, so grep -n '<word>' physics-sandbox.metadump.json returns whole entries.

essence.one_sentence: A 2D physics sandbox is a rigid-body world in which a grabbed box is held by its grab point at the pointer and released into real momentum, so the drag must feel like holding an object that still has weight.
essence.summary: Side-view gravity, rotatable boxes, a fixed-step solver, a grab that follows the pointer, and sleeping resting bodies.

formula.full: fixed-step rigid bodies + pointer-following grab + release that keeps momentum + sleeping resting boxes + stacking
formula.essential: rigid boxes with gravity plus a grab that tracks the pointer

poles: box follows the pointer at once
boxes in a stack keep their contacts

task.is: a 2D physics sandbox where boxes can be dragged around (interactive simulation in a browser or app)
ladder: 2D rigid-body dynamics (gravity, collision, friction, restitution, sleeping)
direct manipulation of simulated bodies (grab, drag, release, throw)
this sandbox's step rate, grab mechanism, constants and states
job: release it and watch it fall, bounce or throw
see it collide and stack with the others

readings.reading: full toy: drag, throw, stacking, reset, several boxes at once

k-prompt-sandbox.text: The output is a 2D physics sandbox.

k-prompt-boxes.text: The objects in the sandbox are boxes.

oq-grab-spring-values.default: tight: hertz 8.0, damping ratio 0.9, max force 6500 from the sourced example

p-drag-boxes.text: A user can drag boxes around inside the sandbox.

ladder_primer._about: Discipline primer for the rungs of the physics-sandbox ladder: simulation and game physics, 2D rigid-body dynamics, direct manipulation.

rp-tunneling.text: Fast bodies can pass through thin walls or floors between steps.
behaviors: A thrown box crosses a neighbour in one step and never collides
rp-tunneling.principle: Bounded step size and speed limits keep contacts detected.
signals: boxes passing through other boxes or the floor

rp-semi-implicit-euler.text: Update velocity from forces first, then position from the new velocity.
behaviors: Stays stable at game step sizes where explicit Euler gains energy
rp-semi-implicit-euler.principle: Using the new velocity for position keeps the integrator stable and cheap.

rp-sleeping.text: Bodies at rest for a time stop being simulated until woken by contact or input.
behaviors: A resting stack stops jittering and saves steps
rp-sleeping.principle: Skipping settled bodies removes resting jitter and cost.

rp-drag-release.text: Follow the pointer while held, then give the body the pointer velocity on release.
behaviors: Release without velocity makes the box drop dead instead of throwing
rp-drag-release.principle: Direct manipulation feels right when the object keeps the motion of the hand.

rp-common-mistakes.text: Variable dt, no step cap, drag by teleporting position, and losing the pointer on leave.
behaviors: Teleporting a box while dragging makes it pass through others
rp-common-mistakes.principle: Drive the body through the simulation so contacts still resolve.

rp-pointer-capture.text: Captured pointer events keep going to the grabbed element while the drag lasts.
behaviors: A fast drag that leaves the box keeps moving it until pointerup
rp-pointer-capture.principle: Capture keeps the grab alive when the pointer leaves the element.
signals: drag stops when the cursor leaves the box

specifics._about: Specific rungs for a 2D draggable-box sandbox: engine facts, typical values, and how grab and sleep are exposed. Quotes are from fetched pages; search-snippet facts are inferred.

sp-substeps.text: Box2D takes a time step and a sub-step count; the recommended sub-step count is 4 at a 1/60 s step.
behaviors: More sub-steps give finer contact and joint response at more CPU cost; long joint chains need more

sp-gravity.text: Box2D's own example sets world gravity to -10 on the y axis; Box2D has no built-in up-vector.
behaviors: Y-up with -10 pulls boxes down at 10 units per second squared; a large gravity magnitude can decrease stability

sp-matter-stiffness.text: Matter.js's MouseConstraint uses a soft constraint whose default stiffness is about 0.1 per a source snippet; the fetched source page was too thin to confirm it.
behaviors: A soft spring lets the box lag behind the pointer and wobble when stacked

sp-step-rate.text: Step with a fixed dt of 1/60 s, advance in dt-sized steps, and carry leftover time in an accumulator. The arcade example ignores frame time.
behaviors: A variable dt makes results vary from run to run, which is harder to debug
sp-step-rate.principle: A fixed step keeps the simulation deterministic and independent of frame rate.

sp-sleep.text: Box2D puts resting bodies to sleep at very little CPU cost, on by default and switchable per world or body. The arcade example comments its sleep call out, so its boxes stay awake.
behaviors: A sleeping body wakes when an awake body touches it, so a grab can wake a stack
A body created asleep ignores its isAwake flag if enableSleep is false
sp-sleep.principle: Sleep saves simulation time for resting bodies; wake-up on contact keeps stacks correct.

interaction._about: Grab, drag, release and contact during a drag, for a 2D box sandbox. Builds on int-drag-grab, int-release-velocity, sc-defold-grab-mechanism and rp-pointer-capture.

heading_path: Pymunk Physics Engine - Stacks of Boxes

int-drag-grab.text: A left press picks the shape under the cursor; motion moves its body to the pointer, and each update pins it again with zero velocity.
behaviors: Held box follows the mouse by setting its position every frame
Gravity is cancelled for the held box by zeroing its velocity after each step
signals: position set from mouse x, y

heading_path: Pymunk Physics Engine - Stacks of Boxes

int-release-velocity.text: While dragging, the box's velocity is set to the pointer motion times 20; release only clears the held shape.

sc-defold-release-gap.term: release and momentum (not in this page)
sc-defold-release-gap.text: The page shows pointer input driving the target but has no release handler and no throw velocity code, so release momentum is undefined in this example.
behaviors: After the first pointer input, user_control stays true and the auto-moving target stops
sc-defold-release-gap.principle: Momentum on release comes from the physics step after the joint stops being driven, which this example never sets up.

f-sleep-tint.text: Sleep events mark bodies at rest; the example tints a sleeping body red and returns it to normal when moved.

inv-grab-under-pointer.term: grab keeps the box under the pointer
inv-grab-under-pointer.invariant: grab keeps the box under the pointer
inv-grab-under-pointer.variable: grab offset in px, from the grab point on the box to the pointer
inv-grab-under-pointer.text: While held, the grab point on the box stays at the pointer, within a small lag that the grab mechanism allows.
signals: box lags the cursor by a few px, then catches up
box never leaves the cursor far behind

int-grab-methods.text: Three ways to hold a box, with a tradeoff between direct control and stacking stability.
options: set position each frame: exact, but a stack above it gets shoved and can sink
spring-damper mouse joint to a static anchor: the box stretches, overshoots and settles
pointer constraint or mouse spring (the Matter.js style): same feel as a joint
behaviors: Setting position ignores contacts, so the held box passes through what it lands on
A softer spring lags more and rebounds more
queries: mouse joint vs set position drag

int-pointer-events.text: Use pointerdown to pick the box, pointermove to follow, pointerup to release, and capture the pointer so a fast drag keeps the box.
properties: pointerdown picks the body under the cursor
behaviors: Without capture, a drag that leaves the box drops it
A second pointer while one box is held starts a second grab or is ignored
queries: multi touch drag ignore second pointer
signals: events keep firing after the cursor leaves the canvas

int-failure-feel.term: drag failures that read as broken
int-failure-feel.text: Failures a player notices first while dragging.
properties: box sinks into the floor under the pointer
behaviors: A spring too stiff for the step size jitters
A grab that sets position every frame jumps when the frame rate changes
int-failure-feel.principle: The grab feels honest when the box moves by forces, not by jumps.

f-drag-mouse-spring.text: Matter.js examples grab a body with a pointer constraint or mouse spring; a cloth demo pins its top row and lets the spring pull the free particles.
signals: mouse spring enabled in the demo

sc-defold-grab-mechanism.text: The grab is a mouse joint between an invisible static anchor body and the dragged dynamic body, not a direct position set.
behaviors: The body stretches, overshoots and settles instead of jumping to the pointer
The soft setting lags behind the pointer and the tight one follows closely
sc-defold-grab-mechanism.principle: A spring toward the target keeps the stack stable where teleporting the body would not.

sc-defold-body-setup.text: Grabbed bodies have gravity off, fixed rotation and linear damping 1.5, so the grab is the main visible force.
behaviors: Linear damping stops the body sliding forever after the target moves
sc-defold-body-setup.principle: Remove other forces so the joint's pull is easy to read.

int-release-throw.text: On release the box keeps the velocity it got while dragged, so a flick throws it.
properties: multiplier of about 20 in the scraped example
behaviors: A fast flick throws the box across the sandbox
Release with zero velocity drops the box dead
int-release-throw.principle: The box keeps the hand's motion so a throw reads as physical.

int-pass-through.text: A held box can push the boxes it meets or pass through them; contact handling decides which.
options: collide: the held box shoves the stack and the stack reacts (the solver resolves contacts)
ghost: the held box ignores other boxes while dragged (no shoving, no stacking feel)
collide with sub-stepping: pushes are kept and fast throws do not tunnel
behaviors: A thrown box crosses a neighbour in one step if the step is too coarse
signals: box visibly sinks into a neighbour
box crosses another with no contact

simulation._about: Simulation rung for a 2D draggable-box sandbox: step rate and integration, collision response, gravity, friction and restitution, sleeping, and failure modes. Sourced values come from the researched entries they build on; the rest are labeled. Options are options, not requirements.

options._about: options, not requirements: choices where nothing decides it

sim-opt-engine.text: Use Box2D, Matter.js or planck.js for stacking and sleep for free; hand-roll to learn the solver. Tradeoff: size and control against collision quality.

sim-opt-step.text: Accumulator with fixed 1/60 s for determinism, or variable dt for simplicity. Tradeoff: repeatable results against less code.

f-render-debug.text: Matter.js debug options draw extra overlays for checking a simulation.

sim-gravity-friction-restitution.text: Two value sets are sourced: a Box2D example gravity of -10 m/s^2 on y, and a pymunk box example with friction 0.9 and elasticity 0.2 on 32 px boxes. A sandbox in screen pixels needs its own gravity scale.
behaviors: Gravity in pixels scales with the chosen pixel-per-meter ratio; change one and retune the other
Friction near 0.9 holds stacks; a low friction lets them slide
sim-gravity-friction-restitution.principle: Pick a world scale first, then express gravity, size and friction in it.

sim-sleep-option.text: Sleep bodies that stay below a speed threshold for a short time, and wake them on any contact or grab.
behaviors: A grab or a box dropped on a sleeping stack should wake every body it touches
Sleep off costs CPU and is simpler to debug
sim-sleep-option.principle: Sleep saves work on resting bodies; wake on contact keeps stacks correct.
signals: idle sandbox drops to near-zero step cost

sim-failure-modes.term: failure modes that make a sandbox feel broken
sim-failure-modes.text: Tunneling (a fast box passes through a thin one), jitter (resting stacks buzz), and sinking (boxes slowly drop into the floor or each other) are the three that make the toy feel broken.
properties: box passing through box while dragged
behaviors: A dragged box moved by position set each frame can pass through others; a fast throw makes this worse
Too few solver iterations let stacks sink
sim-failure-modes.principle: Each failure traces to speed, step size, iterations or missing position correction; check the cause before tuning feel.

sim-collision-response.text: Resolve each contact with an impulse along the contact normal, then correct residual overlap by position projection so boxes separate without bouncing forever.
behaviors: Restitution near 0 makes boxes settle; a higher value makes them bounce on contact
Positional correction without a slop band jitters resting stacks
sim-collision-response.principle: Impulses fix velocity, projection fixes position; both are needed to rest a stack without sinking or jitter.
signals: contact points stay on the surface

sim-box-body.term: box and floor values from a pymunk example

heading_path: Pymunk Physics Engine - Stacks of Boxes

sim-box-body.text: The pymunk example uses 32 by 32 boxes of mass 1.0 with friction 0.9 and elasticity 0.2, a floor with friction 10 at y 80, gravity (0, -900) and 35 solver iterations.

f-gravity-zero.text: Matter.js can run with zero gravity so bodies stay put until pushed; more solver iterations keep a crate stack stable.
behaviors: More solver iterations keep a crate stack stable

sim-integration.text: Advance the world in fixed 1/60 s steps with an accumulator, and run several solver sub-steps per step for stacks.
behaviors: Velocity updates before position in semi-implicit Euler, which keeps falling boxes energy-stable at this step
Raising the sub-step count stiffens stacks at CPU cost
sim-integration.principle: A fixed step keeps the sandbox deterministic and frame-rate independent; sub-steps buy contact stability.
signals: same drop gives same result on any frame rate

scope._about: Readings of the sandbox request, side by side. No reading is the finished deliverable; the consumer picks or combines them. Defaults are marked, nothing else is ranked.

scope-options._about: options, not requirements: builder choices where the prompt and evidence are silent

opt-engine-or-hand.text: Either a 2D engine (Matter.js, Box2D, planck.js) or a small hand-rolled solver; the choice is open and both are listed.

scope-play-level.text: 'Physics sandbox with draggable boxes' reads three ways, from the narrowest to the widest.
behaviors: Release with pointer velocity makes the drag-only reading feel like a throw, not a drop
scope-play-level.principle: The job runs from seeing boxes at rest to resetting, so the full toy covers every step; narrower readings are subsets.

scope-box-shape.text: 'Boxes' reads as one of three shapes.

includes: box can tip and rest on its corner
boxes as one kind among circles or polygons

signals: a box visibly tips when grabbed off-centre
boxes settle flat in a stack
scope-box-shape.principle: Rotatable rectangles are the least narrow reading that still reads as boxes.

scope-view.text: '2D' reads as a top-down plane or a side view with gravity.

includes: boxes drift and stop by friction

behaviors: Without gravity a released box never comes to rest on its own
scope-view.principle: Gravity is what makes release, rest and stacking visible.

readings.in_practice: high linear damping and large mass; a dragged box drags its neighbours and settles slowly
low damping and quick settle; little overshoot, boxes stop where they land
signals: stacks settle within about a second

readings.in_practice: high restitution; boxes rebound off the floor and each other
